title: How can a solo developer turn AI character art into a reusable animated character without an artist?
author: yaxir
selftext:
I am making a 2D action game in Unity without an artist or animator. I generate my character artwork with ChatGPT and other image generators, and I want to turn designs I like into characters I can properly control and animate.

The goal is an editable character that can run, crouch, jump, shoot, take hits and die while keeping the same face, proportions, clothing and held props. I want expressive whole-body movement, with convincing hair and clothing motion. The final output would be detailed pixel sprites, around 124 pixels tall when standing.

I want to keep that character source and use it for new actions and revisions. Generating each animation separately makes consistency difficult.

What workflow gives someone in my position the best chance of achieving this: a constructed 2D rig, image-to-3D followed by rigging, or a hybrid?

I rely heavily on AI assistance and scripting. Which parts can those realistically handle, and which still require skilled drawing, modelling, weight painting or animation work?

If you have completed this, a tutorial or example showing the original artwork, the editable character and several finished animations would be extremely helpful. I am trying to understand the complete process and the remaining manual work.

For local workflows, I have Windows, an RTX 5080 16 GB and about 32 GB RAM. Quantized options are welcome.

I've had good experiences with chatGPT sol 6.1. I've also had bad experiences... Yesterday I got it to create a character, and animated it jumping and hanging on to something , hitting something and rolling. I used the new gif creator for some of these things, and just normal image creator for others. I always attached the original sprite sheet it created with the prompt. It is definitely getting better.

Saying that. I also tried to get it to create some consistently proportioned playing cards and it struggled with that. So it's swings and roundabouts.

comments.author: Berndog25
comments.body:
One decent workflow to start with, that allows reusability, is creating low poly animated meshes, creating a character reference sheet by brainstorming with the AI of your choice, give the reference sheet back to the AI when you ask it to create either a texture atlas, or separate textures to cover your mesh with (specify what type of model you are putting these onto, so your AI can infer best practices). Then comes the hard part, getting those textures onto the model, an artform in itself that can't be summarized by a quick sentence.

Once you have that made, the whole thing, as well as most of its separate parts will be extremely reusable and customizable (especially if you have separate meshes or texture atlas variations which reuse the same texture coordinates for each part you may want to customize or swap out).

comments.author: Own_Badger6076
comments.body: Start learning how to do the different things associated with your game development. People say stupid shit like "I'm not artistic" all the time, but getting good at art is just like any other skill. So spend some time on that skillset to whatever degree you want to be able to say "I made this".
